To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we present DisentanGAIL, a new imitation learning algorithm that is robust to domain differences and is able to efficiently learn directly from expert demonstrations in a shared feature space.
1) DisentanGAIL learns to imitate in a wide range of environments, 2) it is robust to domain differences, and 3) it is able to perform zero-shot transfer.
1) We introduce a new algorithm that enables imitation learning from observations of the expert's environment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing imitation learning algorithms that are more robust to domain differences, while being able to generalize to unseen environments and agent embodiments.

the following questions: How can we enable an autonomous agent to learn from demonstrations in a way that allows it to generalize across different domains? What are the key factors that make an imitation learning algorithm robust across domains?

the following questions: (1) What are the necessary conditions to enable a learning algorithm to imitate from visual demonstrations? (2) How to design an imitation learning algorithm that is robust to differences between expert and learner's domains?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DisentanGAIL is a domain-robust imitation learning algorithm which learns a shared representation of the task being imitated, and is able to generalize across different domains.
our proposed algorithm is able to learn from high-dimensional visual observations of experts, while being able to disregard the differences between the domains of the agent and the expert.
the proposed method is capable of learning a robust policy from a single demonstration of an expert in a different domain, without requiring any prior knowledge of the task or the expert.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

our algorithm enables agents to learn from demonstrations of a single task performed by an expert in one domain, and to successfully imitate in a variety of other domains, without the need of additional data or domain adaptation.

we are the first to show that imitation learning is domain-robust when using adversarial learning with latent variables, and we are the first that shows that mutual information constraints on the discriminator's latent variables are useful in imitation learning.
we are the first to propose a GAIL-based algorithm that can learn to imitate directly from high-dimensional visual demonstrations, without the need for any domain-specific knowledge.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, by disentangling the latent space of the discriminator, we can learn a representation that is invariant to the domain and can be successfully used to imitate in a wide range of tasks.
it is possible to learn robust visual imitation policies by disentangling the information that is relevant for the completion of a task from other domain-dependent information.
it is possible to learn to imitate by observing demonstrations from a different domain, without the need for a full set of expert actions.
